Major GPU architectures arrive approximately every 24 months–Ampere (2020), Hopper (2022), Blackwell (2024), Rubin (expected 2026), each bringing substantial enhancements in GPU logic, memory efficiency, AI acceleration, and power consumption. Between these major architecture updates, NVIDIA now releases new GPUs within the architectural families annually. content.title: The best gaming upgrade in 2026 isn't hardware, it's AI upscaling and frame generation

In fact, when I upgraded from the RTX 3090 to the 4090 in 2022, I saw roughly a 60–70% FPS uplift across the board at 4K. Fast-forward to 2026, and its successor, the RTX 5090, is only about 27% faster for a 25% increase in MSRP.

Even though DLSS 3, which shipped with my RTX 4090, was significantly better than earlier versions, it still wasn't perfect. That changed when Nvidia rolled out DLSS 4 in early 2025. The image looked almost as good as native rendering and sometimes even better than native 4K with TAA enabled. In 2026, we have DLSS 4.5, which takes things even further. Now, I don't even have to stick to the Quality preset to get an image that looks just as good as native. I could use the Balance or Performance mode with Preset L, which manages to reconstruct detail better than Preset M without over-sharpening the image. Even AMD's FSR 4.1 handles motion better than FSR 4, with noticeably less smearing and improved reconstruction of fine detail. All in all, upscaling no longer feels like a compromise. So there's no point sacrificing frame rates by chasing native 4K rendering. ... The RTX 40-series was the first line of GPUs that supported DLSS frame generation.

For PC gamers, getting a significant performance boost has always come down to better hardware, whether that's a faster GPU, a newer CPU, or sometimes even more RAM. In fact, when I upgraded from the RTX 3090 to the 4090 in 2022, I saw roughly a 60–70% FPS uplift across the board at 4K. Fast-forward to 2026, and its successor, the RTX 5090, is only about 27% faster for a 25% increase in MSRP. That felt underwhelming to me, which is why I decided to skip this generation altogether, and as it turns out, it was probably the best decision I made. While nothing has changed in terms of raw horsepower, I'd argue that my 4090 has improved a lot since I bought it four years ago. And it all comes down to software, specifically AI upscaling and frame generation. DLSS has reached a point where I struggle to tell the difference from native rendering, even in motion, and frame generation builds on that by smoothing out performance in a way hardware alone can't.

However, what has changed in recent years is just how much you can get out of your aging hardware before feeling the need to upgrade. Look at the RTX 20-series GPUs, for example. **What is Vera Rubin?**

It's not just a GPU. Nvidia no longer sells chips — it sells racks. The Vera Rubin Superchip combines the Vera CPU and two Rubin GPUs into a single module, stacked into the NVL72 rack-scale system. The whole thing is designed as one big coordinated computer. The name comes from the astronomer Vera Cooper Rubin, who discovered dark matter evidence — Nvidia's framing is that this platform illuminates the "dark matter" of unstructured data.

---

**The Rubin GPU itself**

The Rubin GPU features two near-reticle-sized compute tiles on a 3nm TSMC process, 336 billion transistors, and 288GB of HBM4 memory across eight stacks, delivering roughly 13 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth. It hits 50 petaflops of compute for inference — 5x Blackwell — and 35 petaflops for training.

---

**What is HBM4?**

HBM stands for High Bandwidth Memory. The key thing to understand is that normal RAM sits separate from the chip and data travels to it over a relatively narrow bus. HBM is stacked directly on top of or right next to the processor die on the same package, with a massively wider connection.

HBM4 doubles the interface width compared to HBM3e, and through new memory controllers and tighter compute-memory integration, the Rubin GPU nearly triples memory bandwidth compared to Blackwell. In real numbers, HBM4 delivers 22 TB/s of memory bandwidth — a 2.8x increase over Blackwell's 8 TB/s. This effectively shatters the "memory wall," allowing large language models to load and process data much faster without bottlenecking the compute cores.

Why does that matter? 288GB of HBM4 per GPU enables inference on models exceeding 1 trillion parameters without the latency penalties of multi-node distribution — previous architectures required distributing that work across multiple racks.

---

**What is NVLink?**

NVLink is Nvidia's proprietary high-speed interconnect that lets multiple GPUs talk to each other directly — bypassing the CPU entirely — at speeds that are orders of magnitude faster than standard PCIe connections.

Think of it this way: PCIe is like a highway between the GPU and the rest of the system. NVLink is a direct wormhole between GPUs. When you have 72 GPUs in a rack trying to share data during model training or inference, how fast they can pass information between each other is a critical bottleneck.

NVLink 6 is rated at 3.6 TB/s of bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth per GPU, with 260 TB/s of total scale-up bandwidth across the NVL72 rack. This proves critical for mixture-of-experts architectures where expert routing decisions must complete within microseconds.

There's also a variant called NVLink-C2C (chip to chip) that connects the Vera CPU directly to the Rubin GPU. That runs at 1.8 TB/s and allows the CPU and GPU to access each other's memory as a single unified address space without the latency penalty of PCIe. Basically the CPU and GPU stop being separate things with a bridge between them and become one coherent memory pool.

---

**The full rack — NVL72**

The NVL72 is Nvidia's rack-scale deployment unit: 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs in a single liquid-cooled rack, delivering 3.6 ExaFLOPS of FP4 inference compute, 20.7 TB of HBM4 memory, and 260 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth. **What is Vera Rubin?**

It's not just a GPU. Nvidia no longer sells chips — it sells racks. The Vera Rubin Superchip combines the Vera CPU and two Rubin GPUs into a single module, stacked into the NVL72 rack-scale system. The whole thing is designed as one big coordinated computer. **The Rubin GPU itself**

---

**What is HBM4?**

HBM stands for High Bandwidth Memory. The key thing to understand is that normal RAM sits separate from the chip and data travels to it over a relatively narrow bus. HBM is stacked directly on top of or right next to the processor die on the same package, with a massively wider connection.

HBM4 doubles the interface width compared to HBM3e, and through new memory controllers and tighter compute-memory integration, the Rubin GPU nearly triples memory bandwidth compared to Blackwell. ---

**What is NVLink?**

NVLink is Nvidia's proprietary high-speed interconnect that lets multiple GPUs talk to each other directly — bypassing the CPU entirely — at speeds that are orders of magnitude faster than standard PCIe connections.

Think of it this way: PCIe is like a highway between the GPU and the rest of the system. NVLink is a direct wormhole between GPUs. When you have 72 GPUs in a rack trying to share data during model training or inference, how fast they can pass information between each other is a critical bottleneck.

NVLink 6 is rated at 3.6 TB/s of bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth per GPU, with 260 TB/s of total scale-up bandwidth across the NVL72 rack. This proves critical for mixture-of-experts architectures where expert routing decisions must complete within microseconds.

That runs at 1.8 TB/s and allows the CPU and GPU to access each other's memory as a single unified address space without the latency penalty of PCIe. Basically the CPU and GPU stop being separate things with a bridge between them and become one coherent memory pool.

**The full rack — NVL72**

The NVL72 is Nvidia's rack-scale deployment unit: 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs in a single liquid-cooled rack, delivering 3.6 ExaFLOPS of FP4 inference compute, 20.7 TB of HBM4 memory, and 260 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth. An NPU is a chip designed *specifically* for neural network inference — not training, inference. Where a GPU is a general parallel processor that happens to be good at AI, an NPU is hardwired for the specific operations neural networks perform: dot products, activation functions, attention heads.
